introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2026. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Question 2 : « Tijani Jihad » compris comme le jihad d'al-Hajj Umar Tall (confrérie Tijaniyya, empire toucouleur), seule lecture historiographique usuelle. Dates de l'historiographie courante : Usman dan Fodio 1754-1817 ; hijra à Gudu en 1804 ; prise d'Alkalawa en 1808 ; Sokoto fondée par Muhammad Bello vers 1809 ; jihad d'Umar proclamé vers 1852 ; Ségou prise en 1861 ; Hamdallahi en 1862 ; mort d'Umar en 1864 ; conquête de Ségou par Archinard en 1890 ; Sokoto prise par les Britanniques en 1903. Aucun chiffre militaire avancé.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Compare and contrast the Sokoto and Tijani Jihads in West Africa during the 19th century.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Sokoto Jihad (begun in 1804 under Usman dan Fodio in Hausaland) and the Tijani Jihad (launched about 1852 by Al-Hajj Umar Tall in the Upper Senegal-Niger region) were the two greatest Islamic reform movements of 19th century West Africa. Both aimed to purify Islam and build Muslim states, but they differed in their brotherhood, their enemies, their organisation and their fate. A comparison shows both similarities and important differences.

**Similarities.**
1. *Religious aims.* Both leaders condemned the mixing of Islam with traditional beliefs and the corruption of rulers, and aimed to establish a state based on Islamic law (Sharia), justice and lighter taxation.
2. *Fulani leadership and scholarship.* Both leaders were Muslim scholars of Fulani/Tukulor origin who had studied widely and who gained followers by preaching. Both used the Arabic language and the idea of jihad (holy war) and hijra (withdrawal) to organise their followers. Both drew on ideas from the wider Islamic world: Umar himself made the pilgrimage to Mecca and spent years in the Muslim world before returning, while the Shehu was a scholar of the Qadiriyya tradition and was inspired by earlier reformers.
3. *Methods.* Both began with preaching and the gathering of disciples, then moved to armed conflict when the existing rulers tried to stop them. Both built armies from committed followers, and attracted people who were discontented with the old rulers (peasants, the Fulani herdsmen, slaves, scholars).
4. *Results.* Both created large empires, spread Islam, increased trade and learning, and used slaves in large numbers in agriculture and in the army. Both depended on the personal prestige of the founder.

**Differences.**
1. *Brotherhood.* The Sokoto Jihad was led in the name of the Qadiriyya brotherhood, whereas Umar belonged to the Tijaniyya, which was more militant and open to all classes; this led to rivalry with Qadiri leaders.
2. *Period and region.* Sokoto began in the early 19th century in Hausaland (modern northern Nigeria) and later spread to Adamawa (including parts of northern Cameroon) and Nupe and Ilorin; the Tijani Jihad began in the middle of the century in the Futa Jallon/Senegal and Niger region (the Western Sudan).
3. *Targets.* Dan Fodio fought the Hausa kings, especially the king of Gobir, accused of oppression and of mixing Islam with pagan practices; Umar's targets included non-Muslim Bambara states such as Segu and also the Muslim Fulani state of Macina (Hamdallahi), which brought him into conflict with other Muslims, such as the Kunta leaders.
4. *European threat.* The Sokoto Jihad took place before the European conquest and the Caliphate faced no European army until the end of the century; Umar, on the other hand, came into direct conflict with the French under Faidherbe, expanding from Senegal (the siege of Medina fort in 1857), and his empire had to resist French advances almost from the start.
5. *Government.* Sokoto developed a stable system: the Shehu's successor Muhammad Bello organised the Caliphate into emirates under emirs appointed by the Caliph at Sokoto, with the Shehu's brother Abdullahi governing the western emirates from Gwandu, and a tradition of writing, taxation and law. This system lasted until the British conquest of 1903 and was even used by the British in indirect rule. The Tukulor empire, by contrast, depended on Umar's personality, military command and the loyalty of his sons and officers; it lacked time to build institutions.
6. *Duration and fate.* The Sokoto Caliphate lasted about a century. Umar disappeared in 1864 in the Bandiagara area while putting down a revolt, and the empire under his son Ahmadu was weakened by revolts and French attack: Segu fell to the French in 1890 and the empire was ended in the 1890s.

**Conclusion.** The two jihads shared the same religious inspiration, the leadership of reforming scholars and the creation of large Muslim states using war and slavery. But Sokoto was the older, better organised and more durable, while the Tijani Jihad, which arose just before European conquest, was shorter-lived and failed to resist French power. Their legacy, however, was the spread of Islam, new states and brotherhoods, which still influence West Africa.
